{"docket_number": "178", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1957", "first_party": "John Russell Crooker, Jr.", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "California", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "Supreme Court of California", "argued": ["1958-04-02T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Is a confession obtained during an interrogation in which the suspect asked for and was denied access to counsel obtained in violation of the suspect’s Fourteenth Amendment right to due process?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

On July 5, 1955, John Russell Crooker was arrested for the murder of his boss with whom he had been having an illicit relationship. For the next fourteen hours, Crooker was sporadically questioned and interrogated in his home and in the West Los Angeles Police Station; he repeatedly asked to meet with an attorney and was told that he could call only after the investigation was over. After fourteen hours of detainment and periodic interrogation, Crooker wrote a full confession to the murder. The next morning, Crooker was asked to orally repeat his confession, but he refused and again asked to speak with an attorney. Crooker was permitted to call his attorney at that point, and from then forward, he was represented by his counsel.

At trial, Crooker argued that his confession was obtained in violation of his Fourteenth Amendment right to due process because his confession was coerced by state authorities, and even if it was given voluntarily, he was denied the right to counsel. The issue of whether Crooker’s confession was voluntary was presented to the jury, which resolved the question against Crooker and convicted him. The Supreme Court of California affirmed.

", "conclusion": "

No. Justice Tom C. Clark delivered the opinion for the 5-4 majority. The Court held that the coercion that might occur from a denial of a specific request for counsel can be negated by factors such as the defendant’s age, intelligence, and education. In this case, Crooker had knowledge of his rights based on the fact that he was a law student and that he refused to answer some questions during interrogation. Additionally, Crooker was informed by the police officer that he didn’t have to answer anything he didn’t want to. Therefore, Crooker’s confession was not coerced. The Court also held that, although Crooker’s confession was made without counsel being present, his awareness of his rights meant that the absence of counsel did not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

Justice Douglas wrote a dissenting opinion in which he argued that the repeated denial of counsel to Crooker was a violation of his Due Process right. Justice Black also argued that the preservation of Due Process should also be applied to pre-trial investigation and therefore that the accused who wants counsel should have one at any time after the arrest. Chief Justice Earl Warren, Justice Black Hugo L. Black, and Justice William J. Brennan, Jr. joined in the dissent.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 178, John Russell Krueger, Jr., petitioner versus the people of the state of California. Mr. Armstrong? Yes, Your Honor. Mr. Chief Justice, Honorable Justices of the Court, we have before us in this case a first-degree murder case in which the petitioner, John Russell Krueger, was sentenced to death. The matter is before this court on two questions, and those questions both turn on due process and are both necessarily interrelated to each other. That is, whether or not the defendant was denied due process by virtue of the investigating officers to have refused to allow him to have counsel after requests had been made, and secondly, whether he was denied due process by the admission into evidence of a confession which was taken after he had been held in custody without counsel for some 14 hours. Now, I won't go through detailed facts because they are set out in briefs, but for the court's benefit, I would like to review the time schedule of the particular day in question, that the defendant was arrested in his apartment shortly after noon on the day of July 5, 1955. He was interrogated in his apartment from noon until approximately 4 o'clock, and then he was taken to the central station of the Los Angeles Police Department, and there was held until a little after 8 o'clock. And from there, he was taken to the West Los Angeles Police Station, and there was interrogated until approximately 3.30 in the morning. At 3.30 in the morning, he wrote and signed a detailed confession, which was the morning of the 6th, Your Honor, yes. And then from there, he was taken by the officers who were investigating the case to the home of the decedent, which was in the neighborhood of Los Angeles known as Bel Air, and there was more questioning until approximately 5.30 in the morning. Then he was taken to a jail cell, and from there, he was taken to the district attorney's office of Los Angeles County in the early afternoon hours. And finally, at 7 o'clock on the evening of the 6th of July, he was taken back to jail, rebooked, and was made available to his attorney. Now, this record, Your Honors, is rather voluminous, and I apologize for it, and at the same time, you should have seen it before we cut it down, because we have digested it from over 2,000 pages, and so I will make some necessary references to it, and then try to stay away from having to tie the court's attention to the record. But there are some questions that must necessarily be pointed out, and I feel that the Supreme Court of California overlooked, in its opinion, on the question of the undisputed facts of request for counsel. Now, one of the investigating officers was a Sergeant Gotch, and his testimony on the defendant's request for counsel appears at the transcript of the record, page 83, first establishing the time. He said that they left between 4 and 4.30, the apartment, and went directly to Central Station. So from this, we can infer that the time was about 5 o'clock, and we have this testimony on page 83. Question 3. What is the first time that the defendant said anything to you about wanting to call an attorney? Answer. I believe the first time, to the best of my recollection, was after we'd given him the sandwich and a bottle of milk, and had given him time to consume that and smoke a cigarette. He was in the polygraph room. I'm not sure when he did make a request for an attorney. Question. When he made the request for an attorney, what did you tell him? Answer. I asked him, who did he want? Question. And he said what? Answer. He said he didn't know. Question. What else did he say on this subject? Answer. I stated to him that after our investigation was concluded, he could call an attorney, and if he didn't have funds to hire an attorney when he went to court, a public defender would be assigned. He then stated he had a friend who'd been an instructor at Pepperdine College and would probably handle the case for him. I asked him who the name was, and he said it was a man by the name of Simpson who lived in Long Beach. Question. He asked you if he could call an attorney at that time, and you told him he could call after the investigation was completed. Is that right? I told him that after I was through with the investigation, he could make a call. Now, Your Honor, the significant thing about this testimony is that this is established as being about 5 o'clock in the afternoon. In other words, about 10 hours before the actual confession was gained. Now, also, the transcript of the record on page 134, and I won't bother to read this in its entirety to the court in the interest of time, but on 134, at the bottom of the page, the last question and answer was addressed to the polygraph examiner that they had taken him to and asked him to take this lie detector test, and there again there was discussion of an attorney. Now, this polygraph examiner did not say that he asked for an attorney, but he did admit that he was talking about an attorney. I believe it was a former instructor. So it was identified as the same man, former instructor, who was Mr. Simpson, who comes into this again, who was his instructor at Pepperdine College. And he says, do you remember what you said to him when he asked, when he talked about an attorney? And he said, no, I don't remember. I imagine I state it was his privilege. Then we come to Lieutenant... Do you imagine what? I imagine that I stated it was his privilege. The polygraph examiner said that it was his probable reply. Now, that is a transcript of record, page 134 and 135, Your Honor. Now, the third reference to an attorney was Lieutenant Armstrong, who was one of the officers in charge of the investigation, and we find that at page 71 of the record. And on page 71, this officer was asked, and at the time Officer Willis was explaining the lie detector procedures, do you recall at that time the defendant said to Officer Willis in your presence that he did not wish to take the test until he'd had an opportunity to consult with an attorney? Answer, I don't recall that. He may have said that, but I don't recall that, Mr. Armstrong. This was the reply to me, the two Armstrongs may be confusing, but Lieutenant Armstrong was in charge of the investigation. He says he may have said that. So we have this concession from Lieutenant Armstrong at page 71 of the record. Now, in addition, we have the defendant's testimony that he asked each of these investigating officers, right from the beginning, right from the time they first came into his apartment, he said, may I make a telephone call, may I call an attorney, starting with the officers Kruger and Jackson, who were the initial arresting officers. And then when Sergeant Gotch came on the scene, he renewed the request. So this is his testimony, is that all the way through, he asked for counsel. Now these other officers took the stand and either equivocated or denied the request for attorney. Lieutenant Armstrong again, at pages 66, 70, and 71 of the record, when I asked him, did he say that he wished to get in touch with an attorney, he said, I don't recall that. And on page 70, when he was asked a similar question, now at the time of that conversation, Lieutenant Armstrong, towards the bottom of the page, did the defendant at that time say anything about wanting to confer with an attorney? Not that I recall, Mr. Armstrong. And then I said, may I refresh your recollection? Did he say that he wished to see an attorney before submitting to such a test? Does that help you to recall? I don't recall any request for an attorney counselor. And over in the middle of page 71, he said, I don't recall that. This is the allusion that I've previously made to the transcript. He may have said it, that he didn't want to take the test until he had an attorney, but I don't recall. Then we go to Inspector Kerr, who testified that he talked to him at 11.15 in the evening, considerably later. But that is on page 120 of the record, Your Honor. And here, looking at the answers from the top of the page on down, the first three answers are all, I don't recall anything about an attorney. I don't recall any conversation about an attorney at that time. No, sir, I don't recall any such conversation. And I don't recall any conversation about the attorney. No, sir. Now, these were the inspector's answers. Well, now, the significance of this, Your Honors, is this, is that it is obvious that both of these experienced officers in the Los Angeles Police Department, Inspector Kerr is one of the third-ranking officers in the entire Los Angeles Police Department, subordinate only to the deputy chief, and has been a police officer for many years. Lieutenant Armstrong testified that he'd been a police officer for 20 years. And these officers were familiar with investigative procedures. And the fact that they didn't recall whether a request for an attorney had been made or not was clear evidence of the fact that they didn't care whether a request for an attorney had been made or not because their attitude was the same that Sergeant Gotch came out and said in so many words. And that was, when we're through with you, you can have an attorney, you can make a call. But not until we're through with the investigation. And this was part of the psychological coercion under which this confession was taken because this interrogation went on and on and on. At 2.30 in the morning, there was no indication that it was about to let up. In fact, it didn't let up. And it went on beyond that time. And as this court said, in Haley v. Ohio at 322 U.S. 596, speaking of another subject, but the words are in point here, I believe, it said that these events are not germane to the present problem because they were after the confession, but they show such a callous attitude of police towards the safeguards which respect for ordinary standards of human relationships require that we take with a grain of salt their statements that the five-hour drilling of this boy was done in a fair and dispassionate manner. And so I think in this case, that was from Haley v. Ohio, your Honor, 332 U.S. 596. Now, we have to look at the context of this a little bit, your Honors, and see who was there. This was an important case in Los Angeles County, in Los Angeles City, because of the fact of the social prominence of the victim of this homicide. And so assigned to this case and present at various stages during the investigation were these people. An inspector of police, a captain of police, the head of the crime lab of the Los Angeles Police Department, a lieutenant, three sergeants, five officers, and the chief deputy district attorney were all present at one stage or another, and some of them all the way through as this investigation went on. Thirteen men arrayed against one man while this investigation was going on, and of each of these, the defendant said, that he requested an attorney. He said, I don't care to discuss that until I've had an opportunity to confer with an attorney. I don't want to talk about that until I can see an attorney. When can I see an attorney? He asked each of them. Now, only Willis admits that he had talked about an attorney at all. The others denied it completely or else said they didn't recall. The two senior men on the police department in this investigation, Inspector Kerr and Lieutenant Armstrong, said they had no recollection. The sergeant who was in charge of the investigation, Sergeant Gotch, gave us the only direct testimony about an actual conversation and a request for an attorney and what he was told. But the point is, is that that conversation was ten hours before the confession was actually taken from him. Now, as far as physical abuse is concerned, the defendant testified at page 161 of the record that Sergeant Hooper, at one point in the questioning, about 2.30 in the morning, came up to him and banged him on the knee and said, we're sick and tired of these evasive answers or words to this effect, and then punched him in the stomach and said, we're going to get some straight answers out of here, we're going to work you over all night, and then punched him in the stomach again. Now, this is what the defendant's testimony was. Sergeant Hooper was called by the people, and he unequivocally denied this. This was at page 243 of the record. Did all this evidence go before the jury? Yes, Your Honor, it did. However, Your Honor, the significant thing is this, is that in the district attorney's office, there was a transcript made of all the proceedings in the district attorney's office, and all the proceedings in there were both taken down by a stenotypist and were also wire recorded. And in the district attorney's office, the defendant said these things, which gave the lie to some of these other officers' testimony. He said to district attorney Roll, everybody here knows this. I've been requesting counsel since this case started, and I just want to know when I can get an attorney. And this assertion of him, in the presence of the officers, the officers were right there at the beginning of the statement, which was people's proposed exhibit 29, which was excluded from evidence in part, but part of it went before the jury. In this proposed exhibit, the district attorney Roll started out by saying, well, for the record, let's all identify ourselves. Go around the room. Lieutenant Armstrong, Sergeant Gotch, Deputy District Attorney Alexander, Officer Stambler. Here were the officers that had been conducting this interrogation. They were all there, and the defendant said, and these officers made frequent interruptions in the process of this transcript. Whenever they felt like saying something, they spoke right up. And the defendant said to Mr. Roll, I'm sure everybody here knows it. I've been requesting counsel, and I'd like to know when I can finally get one. And there wasn't a demur to it. Now, here is the more important thing on the physical abuse. The defendant said, and this was his testimony, and we knew at the time that he said this, that everything in that district attorney's office was recorded. The recording was not available to the defense. The entire transcript was not available to anybody because of the fact that the court struck it after the fact that it was determined that district attorney Roll had eavesdropped on a conversation between the defendant and the counsel that he was finally allowed to call. And from that point on, from the request for attorney, the judge said, we cut it off there so we didn't get to see the rest of it. But the defendant testified at the trial. I said to district attorney Roll, he, indicating Sergeant Hooper, hit me. He hit me twice in the stomach. And Mr. Hooper's reply was, I don't believe we hurt you. And he says, I don't care what you think, you hit me. You hit me twice in the stomach, and again, Sergeant Hooper said, I don't believe we hurt you. This appears at 204 of the record. Now, the people had the power to controvert this, even though the exhibit had been excluded because we availed ourselves of it when we caught Sergeant Hooper in an untruth and we came to an impeaching part of the testimony as we've set out in the briefs. The district attorney objected and said, oh no, you can't impeach him because this is excluded record. And the judge said, I will not allow an untruthful witness to take sanctuary behind the ruling of a court. Go ahead and ask your impeaching question. And they could have done the same. And so if Hooper had not been telling the truth about what was said in the district attorney's office, they had the power to come up and say this wasn't true. You weren't hit after all. You're just saying this. And it isn't even so. So this can be impliedly taken as true by virtue of the failure of the people to rebut this particular testimony. Now, in the... There wasn't necessarily a conflict, a decided conflict, as far as this evidence went and what the police officers said and what the defendants said. And I would call this court's attention respectfully to the case of Ashcraft v. Tennessee on this particular subject, where the court said, such disputes, we may say, are the inescapable consequence of secret inquisitorial practices and always evidence concerning the inner details of secret inquisitions is weighted against an accused, particularly where, as here, he is charged with a brutal crime. And that's exactly the situation that we had before us in this case. Now, in the... As far as the evidence in the district attorney's office is concerned, this is material for the same... for the same reason of the language of Haley v. Ohio that I've previously cited this court, in that it showed the callous disregard for these law enforcement officers because when the district attorney finally allowed the defendant in the office in the presence of all these people to use the telephone and to call an attorney, he got on the line himself and listened to the conversation and interrupted it four times to intersperse his own remarks and to say what he wanted to say. And when the defendant said to his counsel, they're making me say things, they're using force on me, the district attorney got on the phone and he said, Mr. Simpson, you know that isn't true. And four separate occasions, he came out with exactly... with interruptions in the testimony or interruptions in the conversation between the defendant and his attorney. And then, the district attorney had the audacity at the trial to tell the court that it was his intention to play a wire recording of the entire proceedings. And as I've set forth in the briefs, the questions of the district attorney show specifically that the entire telephone conversation was recorded illegally in the district attorney's office. Now, the significance of this, Your Honor, is that here was this defendant who had had a bad time with the police all night the night before, who'd requested counsel again and again and again and had his request denied. And this man had reason to believe that here, in the chief law enforcement officer's office of Los Angeles County, he could find some sanctuary that here his rights would be respected. And I submit to Your Honors that here was the most callous disregard of all. And it was for this reason, of course, that the court stepped in. And the court said, we're not going to let any of this come in. And I think the court's comments on this particular point at page 341 of the record are... 341 of the record are indicative of what kind of conduct had been going on. The court says, now, the court has always had high regard for the ethical standards of the office of the district attorney. However, the conduct of the district attorney and listening to the defendant's conversation with an attorney, interrupting the conversation on an extension phone, is highly improper for a law enforcement officer who is a member of the law. So the court excursionated the district attorney for this conduct, but the damage had been done. And the fact that the chief deputy district attorney who was present during the investigative stages of this case was also present during this portion of the case shows the attitude that sets the tone of the investigation. And that's why the Haley language is so particularly important. Now, we have here the fact that this confession, taken after... Mr. Armstrong, may I ask... I assume that the defendant had no knowledge of the fact that there was a recording being made in the district attorney's office? Absolutely not. And at the beginning, at least, he had no knowledge of the fact that the district attorney was on the telephone, extension telephone? I don't believe he was aware of it, Your Honor. It was in the same room. He became aware of it very shortly because it was after practically his open remark. You see, the district attorney placed the call and talked to Mr. Simpson and said, well, here's Mr. Crooker. He's here now. You can talk to him and then handed the instrument to Mr. Crooker. Then the district attorney went over and got on an extension. Now, I don't know whether Mr. Crooker noticed that or not, but he became aware of it very soon because it was after practically the opening remark that the district attorney interrupted the conversation. Is there anybody else in the room besides the two of them? Oh, yes, Your Honor. The whole investigative force of the police department. Chief Deputy District Attorney Alexander was there. Dr. Marcus Cran, the jail physician, was there. Gotch was there. Stammer was there. Armstrong was there. All these investigating officers had been in the whole thing. You see, he was still in the midst of all of them. And the district attorney was teaming up with the same type of tactics that had been going on all night the night before. Now, the significant thing that happened here was that after all these facts had come into evidence, the judge nevertheless ruled that the jury might consider this confession for whatever reason that they wanted to. And the question, as we set out in the brief, that the foreman of the jury directed to the court after the jury retired indicated that this question as to whether or not he'd been denied counsel after request was resolved in our favor because the foreman came out and said, what do we do if we find that he did request counsel and counsel was denied him? And this was when we got the watered-down instruction from the court repeated of which we had first complained. But this is merely a fact or circumstance which you can take into consideration. And so, as far as the cases that the respondent has cited, Your Honors, to the fact that this court should not go beyond the supervisorial powers that they can exercise in other federal courts and take the ball away from the state court in this case, it's our contention that they're inapplicable because the facts were determined in our favor. It was the conclusions that were drawn from the facts of which we complained and which we asked this court to reexamine under the authority of Ashcraft versus Tennessee, Powell versus Alabama, Watts versus Indiana, Harris versus South Carolina, and many, many other cases where this court has held that it has the power to reexamine facts if they feel that due process has been violated. Your Honors, I'm anxious to reserve a small portion of time for reply, so I will stop at this point and conclude after hearing from you. You may, Mr. Armstrong. Mr. James. Thank you, the Honor. Honorable Chief Justice and Honorable Associate Justices of the Supreme Court of the United States, those of us in California whose responsibility is the enforcement of the criminal law are very much concerned and most keenly aware of the tremendous responsibility resting upon us by reason of the two questions to which this court has limited its consideration of this matter. Although they have been mentioned by Mr. Armstrong, I think I should repeat them because I want to refer to the first question. The first read, was the defendant denied due process of law by the refusal of the investigation officers to allow him to consult with an attorney upon demand being made to do so while he was in custody and the second, was the defendant denied due process of law by the admission into evidence of a confession which was taken from him while in custody and after he'd been in custody for 14 hours and had not been allowed to consult with his attorney. Before you, may I interrupt this very point? To put this to you, if it's the planet out to you, before you go into the discussion of the law, so-called, of legal consideration, would you take two or three minutes to state what in your view, what in your view, are the conceited, what you concede to be the questions of fact from which any legal consideration, to which legal considerations must be addressed? Yes, I would be... What is it that you, as to which you agree, we may take without question the basis of consideration what legal requirements flow from them? Perhaps, Your Honor, I will digress from my original plan of argument and discuss the fact situation, Just state it without argument, but you accept as... We accept the fact this man was under arrest for a vicious murder that during this period of time, the... According to the accepted testimony of the police officers, there was no force or coercion or threat of coercion asserted upon him. We concede that at one period, one time, he discussed an attorney, as indicated with the conversation with Sergeant Gotch, there was a reference when he was discussing the polygraph by Willis, the polygraph operator. Now, that's a reference to an attorney. Our position is that that mere reference itself, the request, if that's what you call it, for an attorney, does not foreclose any further examination by this court into the whole circumstances, the total facts of this case, to ascertain the question whether this defendant was denied due process of law... How long was the inquiry by all law-enforcing officers? Over what period? I'll briefly summarize what I believe. He was arrested at about 1.30 in the afternoon of July the 5th. He was in his apartment until about 3.30 when some other officers arrived, and as I recall, he was taken by Sergeant Gotch to the Central Station around 4.30, as I recall, 4 to 4.30, and he arrived at the Central Station in downtown Los Angeles about 5.15 to 5.30 in the afternoon, and he was taken to the photo lab where he was photographed. At about 6.30, he was taken to the polygraph room where he talked with Willis, the operator, for a period of about an hour and a half. At this time, he was brought sandwiches, some milk, and left alone to eat it without any questioning. Now, up to this time, they'd only asked him a few questions because, as I believe it was Inspector Care pointed out, the purpose at this time was not to question and defend him when there was a possibility that he might consent to a lie detector test. So they weren't interrogating him concerning the crime. They'd asked him a few questions how he got his hands injured, and he told him a lie, and they questioned him further, and they asked him if he'd been on Samara Road where the residence of the deceased was located, and he lied about that and said no, and later on, they asked him why he'd lied, and he said he declined to answer. Now, subsequent to that time, he was interrogated for Baranau, as the record reveals, and then about 9.30 on July the 5th in the evening, he was taken to West Los Angeles, a trip which takes about a half an hour. He arrived at West Los Angeles at about 10 to 10.30 p.m., and he was next questioned at West Los Angeles from about 11 o'clock to about 12 o'clock midnight. He was then booked by Gotch, a procedure which takes about 20 to 45 minutes. No questioning took place during this period. He was then returned to the detective bureau where he was examined by a doctor, and then he was interrogated and questioned from 1.15 to about 2 a.m., a period of about 45 minutes, and then from 2 a.m., he was left alone with Officer Gravati, and between the time of 2.15 to about 3.30, he sat down and he wrote the confession, which is People's Exhibit 18. Now, does that include the time period? No, that brings it up to the confession, Your Honor. Subsequent of that time, about 3.30 in the morning, he was taken to the scene of his crime, which took about a half an hour from the West Los Angeles Station, and there he showed the officers where he had stayed in the closet and so forth and so on. I think he was there about half an hour. Then he was returned, as I recall, to the detective bureau, and at about 5 o'clock in the morning. And as Mr. Armstrong has related, this was on July 6. He is in the district attorney's office in the afternoon of July 6. That is when the phone call is made to the attorney in Long Beach, and then he is, I believe, brought to the West Los Angeles Station where he confers with his attorney at about 7 o'clock at night. Now, as I get it, from 1.30 to 8, there were no, was there any disclosure made during that period which was introduced in evidence, during the period when it was hoped that he would subject himself to a lie detector? No, except the statements that he had made to the officers concerning the abrasions on his hands, the scratches on his chin, and his statement in regard to not being... Now, during that period when they hoped he'd subject himself to a lie detector, during that period, what in view of the state was the request made by him, if any, that he wanted a lawyer? The testimony of Officer Gotch? What in the view of the state must be conceded and will be conceded is true by you? Yes. Was a statement by him, I'd like to have a lawyer? The testimony of Officer Gotch, and I think it's been read to you, we have detailed it in our brief. Never mind, I just summarized. Yes. We accept that as the statement of the defendant to Gotch. When he made a request or made the statement in regard to an attorney, Gotch asked him who he wanted for an attorney and he said he didn't know. And then he was told his right, he was told that he could, at that time, call an attorney after the investigation was over, and if he didn't have funds to hire an attorney, when he went to court, a public defender would be assigned to handle a case for him. Now, if you were asked whether between 1.30 and 8, the petitioner requested that he be allowed to call an attorney and it was denied him, would you say, yes, that is true? If you can accept Officer Gotch's testimony as such... He's your witness, isn't he? Yes, Your Honor. We accept his statement in regard to the, first, the statement that, regarding to an attorney, the statement he didn't know who he was going to have and then that he had this instructor friend of his in Long Beach who might handle the case for him.
